name: INTEGRATED LAND USE PLANNING FOR LAND DEGRADATION NEUTRALITY
description: This level encompasses the operational frameworks and analytical processes required to guide land users in achieving Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) through science-based and participatory decision-making. It is grounded in the Integrated Land Use Planning (ILUP) approach, which promotes systematic, cross-sectoral, and multi-stakeholder planning based on comprehensive assessments of biophysical resources and socio-economic conditions. Building on these assessments, integrated planning enables the identification of degradation hotspots, the anticipation of land-use trends, and the spatial targeting of context-specific Sustainable Land Management (SLM) practices to balance anticipated losses with planned gains. Robust monitoring systems track global LDN indicators—land cover, productivity, and soil organic carbon—alongside local metrics to validate progress, support adaptive management, and ensure social and environmental safeguards.

name: INTEGRATED, DIVERSIFIED AND RESILIENT PRODUCTION SYSTEMS
description:
This level focuses on the operationalization of long-term integrated strategies through on-the-ground land-interventions that rehabilitate, conserve, and sustainably manage land and water resources. By applying locally led, context specific, and holistic approaches, it seeks to actively avoid, reduce, and reverse the degradation of agricultural lands and soils. The overarching objective is to transition toward sustainable, socioeconomically viable, and resilient agrifood systems grounded in healthy and fertile soils. 
Implementation draws on Ecosystem-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches to establish biodiversity-friendly cropping systems.
The three clusters - Cropland, Grassland, and Supporting ecosystems - should be addressed in an integrated way in order to maximize synergies across activities and ensure coherent, landscape-level outcomes.

name: ENABLING ENVIRONMENT
description: This level comprises four interrelated clusters: Policy Coherence, Markets & Value Chains, Governance of soil, land and water, and Resource Mobilization & Investment. The Enabling Environment represents the combination of contextual elements - encompassing institutional, financial, policy-regulatory, and science-policy dimensions - that are necessary to facilitate progress towards Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN). This level focuses on creating the conditions in which interventions to avoid, reduce, or reverse land degradation can be successfully initiated and implemented, characterized by inclusive policies, sustainable institutions, access to finance, and governance of soil, land and water. It necessitates achieving policy coherence by aligning legal frameworks with international standards and coordinating management strategies across sectors to minimize trade-offs among competing land uses. Furthermore, it requires the Governance of soil, land and water to legally recognize legitimate rights and safeguard vulnerable groups, while simultaneously enhancing market access and infrastructure to support sustainable value chains. Finally, it involves vigorous resource mobilization through financial needs assessments and regulatory frameworks that incentivize public and private investment in innovative, sustainable land management solutions.

name: Assessment
description: This cluster relies specifically on Step 4 of the Integrated Land Use Planning (ILUP). It provides the necessary evidence base to design long-term integrated strategies for the restoration, conservation and sustainable management of land and water resources. It involves characterizing the state and severity of land degradation to inform actions that minimize and reverse desertification. By conducting a systematic inventory of natural capital - including climate, soil, land, and water resources - and evaluating land potential, this cluster is assessment is crucial for the integrated planning activities. It assesses current practices to support the transition to sustainable, socioeconomically viable and resilient agriculture and food systems grounded in healthy and fertile soils. This cluster mandates a comprehensive gender-sensitive analysis of the socioeconomic environment. This analysis examines livelihood strategies, and access to productive resources to address structural inequalities and understand the differential vulnerability of women, youth, and marginalized groups to shocks and stresses. Finally, it integrates biophysical and socioeconomic data to map land uses and stakeholders, utilizing early warning systems to manage risks associated with additional stress on land caused by climate change.
parent: INTEGRATED LAND USE PLANNING FOR LAND DEGRADATION NEUTRALITY
Next activities: Define Vision & Objectives for the Landscape(s)

name: Land-Use planning
description: This cluster supports the development of integrated land use plans that translate assessments and stakeholder priorities into spatially explicit, actionable strategies. Following the Integrated Land Use Planning (ILUP) guidelines, it establishes a shared vision and identifies priority areas by applying the response hierarchy to avoid, reduce and reverse degradation. This involves compiling innovative science-based sustainable solutions and ecosystem-based approaches that are combined with local and traditional practices to ensure locally led, contextually relevant, and holistic approaches. By utilizing spatial analysis to link sustainable land and soil management practices to specific landscapes, this cluster aims to optimize resource use and counterbalance anticipated losses with planned gains. Finally, it operationalizes these interventions through a detailed roadmap to guide implementation and ensure the restoration, conservation and sustainable management of land and water resources.
parent: INTEGRATED LAND USE PLANNING FOR LAND DEGRADATION NEUTRALITY
Next activities: Promote Sustainable Land Management and cropping diversity|Promote Sustainable Grazing Land Management

name: Monitoring and adapting
description: The Monitoring cluster focuses on establishing robust systems to track progress towards land degradation neutrality by measuring trends in land cover, land productivity, and carbon stocks against a fixed baseline to determine net gains and losses. It assesses the performance of sustainable land management and ecosystem restoration by tracking soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and soil health to verify the effectiveness of interventions. Moving beyond single-crop yields, this cluster evaluates sustainable productivity through Total Factor Productivity (TFP) and resource use efficiency to ensure production does not compromise natural capital or ecosystem services. Crucially, it implements comprehensive assessment frameworks to monitor socio-economic impacts, with a specific focus on food security, gender equality, and the resilience of vulnerable communities to shocks and stresses. It also involves participatory monitoring of responsible governance to assess tenure security and the recognition of legitimate rights, particularly for Indigenous Peoples and local communities. Finally, it utilizes early warning systems to conduct continuous vulnerability and risk assessments, tracking hazard exposure and water scarcity to anticipate impacts before they escalate.
parent: INTEGRATED LAND USE PLANNING FOR LAND DEGRADATION NEUTRALITY
Prerequisite activities: Characterize the Land Degradation|Characterize Biophysical Resources

name: Cropland
description: This cluster focuses on implementing diversification strategies to establish drought-resistant cropping systems that support land and soil restoration. The application of Sustainable Land Management (SLM) and Sustainable Soil Management (SSM) harnesses natural processes, promotes beneficial biological interactions and synergies, enhances ecosystem services, and contributes to more diverse, resilient, and productive cropping systems. Increasing crop diversity - including neglected and underutilized species - can improve dietary diversity and nutrition, while also enhancing climate resilience and soil health. The result is more diverse, resilient, and productive cropping systems that contribute to long-term sustainability and improved soil functionality.
parent: INTEGRATED, DIVERSIFIED AND RESILIENT PRODUCTION SYSTEMS
Prerequisite activities: Characterized Biophysical Resources|Prepared inventory of SLM good practices
Next activities: Monitor Sustainable Soil Management Performance|Monitor Sustainable Productivity

name: Grassland
description: This cluster addresses the management of pastures and livestock to prevent land degradation and enhance ecological functions. It includes policy measures to formally support pastoral mobility, recognizing and protecting the collective and customary rights that underpin traditional, flexible grazing land management. It also covers sustainable grazing land management approaches, such as managing grazing pressure (for example, through rotational grazing or rangeland resting), to promote productivity, prevent degradation, and support soil carbon storage.
parent: INTEGRATED, DIVERSIFIED AND RESILIENT PRODUCTION SYSTEMS
Prerequisite activities: Characterized Biophysical Resources|Prepared inventory of SLM good practices
Next activities: Monitor Sustainable Soil Management Performance|Monitor Sustainable Productivity

name: Supporting Ecosystems
description:
This cluster focuses on the application of nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches to sustain land productivity, restore degraded ecosystems, and enhance the resilience of agrifood systems to climate change. These approaches harness ecological processes and biodiversity to deliver multiple co-benefits - supporting climate adaptation and mitigation, improving water and soil health, and strengthening livelihoods. Ecosystem-based solutions in this context include a range of interventions such as agroforestry, integrated watershed and landscape management, and the conservation or restoration of natural habitats within agricultural areas. These practices contribute to the creation of multifunctional landscapes that maintain ecological integrity, enhance ecosystem services, and reduce vulnerability to environmental shocks. By embedding these strategies within broader land-use planning and community-led governance, this cluster reinforces the SLUS principles of systems thinking, participatory decision-making, and integration across land uses.
Ecosystem-based solutions are particularly effective when implemented alongside sustainable cropping and grazing systems, as they provide the ecological foundation - healthy soils, water regulation, biodiversity corridors - upon which productive and resilient agrifood systems depend.
parent: INTEGRATED, DIVERSIFIED AND RESILIENT PRODUCTION SYSTEMS
Prerequisite activities: Characterized Biophysical Resources|Prepared inventory of SLM good practices
Next activities: Monitor Sustainable land and soil management performance|Monitor LDN Achievement and Validate Progress

name: Policy coherence
description: The Policy coherence cluster focuses on establishing long-term strategies for the restoration, conservation and sustainable management of land and water resources to minimize and reverse desertification and land degradation. It entails the systematic alignment of legal frameworks with governance of soil, land and water standards, specifically the Voluntary Guidelines for the Responsible Governance of Tenure (VGGT), to ensure tenure security is not compromised. To minimize trade-offs and maximize synergies, this cluster promotes integrated resources management and the coordination of sustainable land and soil management across sectors to address additional stresses on land. It further advances inclusive governance that integrates local and traditional practices and locally led, contextually relevant, and holistic approaches into decision-making to support biodiversity, drought resilience and food security. In addition, the cluster encourages the strategic alignment of public policies and investments in food and agriculture to ensure that sustainable land use and management are pursued alongside broader social, economic, and environmental objectives, thereby strengthening overall policy coherence across development priorities.
Next activities: Financial needs assessments and budget alignment|Legally recognize and respect all legitimate tenure rights

name: Markets
description: The Market and value chain cluster focuses on the transition to sustainable, socioeconomically viable and resilient agriculture and food systems by strengthening the economic agency of farmers, including smallholders. It emphasizes partnerships and policies that foster rural-urban linkages and support producer organizations, including through public procurement from family farmers. To ensure food security and the reliable supply of nutritious, locally adapted and diverse crops, this cluster prioritizes investments in infrastructure - such as storage facilities and cold chains - to drastically reduce post-harvest losses and enhance the resilience of livelihoods.
Prerequisite activities: Review and Align Policies related to land, soil and water management and tenure|Financial Needs Assessments and Budget Alignment

name: Integrated Governance of soil, land and water
description: This cluster focuses on strengthening integrated governance frameworks that guide the sustainable management of land, soil and water resources. It promotes coherent policy frameworks, inclusive governance structures and transparent institutional arrangements that enable coordinated decision-making across sectors such as agriculture, environment and land-use planning. Guided by internationally recognized frameworks, including the Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of Land, Fisheries and Forests, the World Soil Charter and the Voluntary Guidelines for Sustainable Soil Management, the cluster promotes responsible governance systems that ensure equitable access to land and water resources while safeguarding soil health. It supports the development of inclusive policies, multi-level governance mechanisms and participatory decision-making processes involving governments, civil society, Indigenous Peoples and local communities. Particular attention is given to securing legitimate tenure rights, strengthening gender-responsive land governance and protecting vulnerable groups from dispossession and exclusion. By reinforcing accountability, transparency and coordination across governance levels, these actions aim to prevent land and soil degradation, support sustainable land management and encourage long-term investment in resilient agricultural landscapes.
Prerequisite activities: Review and Align Policies related to land, soil and water management and tenure|Characterize Land Uses and Stakeholders
Next activities: Define Vision & Objectives for the Landscape(s)

name: Resource mobilization and investment
description: The Resource mobilization and investment cluster focuses on establishing the financial enabling environment required to implement long-term integrated strategies for sustainable land management. It emphasizes the need to invest in the development of innovative science-based sustainable solutions and partnerships between public, private, and financial sectors to mobilize capital. To ensure national budgets align with these objectives, this cluster prioritizes conducting financial needs assessments and analyzing public expenditures to redirect subsidies that may be harmful to biodiversity or land health toward investments that yield long-term benefits. It seeks to create a stable and transparent regulatory environment that incentivizes responsible private investment in sustainable agriculture and land restoration while managing risks. Finally, it promotes the use of blended finance mechanisms and de-risking strategies to support investments in Ecosystem-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches, thereby enhancing productivity and resilience.
Prerequisite activities: Review and align policies related to land, soil and water management and tenure
Next activities: Promote Sustainable Land Management and cropping diversity|Monitor Sustainable Land and Soil Management Performance

name: Science and innovation
description:
The Science and Innovation Cluster focuses on the systematic generation, validation, documentation, and sharing of knowledge to support the transition toward sustainable, resilient, and climate-adapted agrifood systems. It strengthens the links between scientific research, policy processes, and local knowledge systems, ensuring that decisions related to land, soil, water, and ecosystem management are evidence-based, inclusive, and responsive to changing environmental conditions.
This cluster promotes the integration of scientific evidence, geospatial data, digital tools, and experiential knowledge from farmers, pastoralists, and Indigenous Peoples to guide sustainable land management and ecosystem restoration. By fostering science–policy interfaces, participatory learning approaches, and knowledge-sharing platforms, it enables stakeholders at multiple scales—from local land users to national policymakers—to access reliable information, co-develop solutions, and scale up effective practices.
Through strengthened monitoring systems, digital innovation, and institutional capacity development, the cluster supports transparent reporting, adaptive management, and the implementation of global commitments related to land degradation neutrality, climate change adaptation, biodiversity conservation, and ecosystem restoration. In doing so, it contributes to efforts to avoid further land degradation, reduce ongoing degradation processes, and reverse degraded ecosystems.
Prerequisite activities: All activities|Characterize the Land Degradation of Agricultural Land|Identification and Prioritisation of Sustainable Land Management
Next activities: Promote Sustainable Land Management and cropping diversity|Monitor Sustainable Land and Soil Management Performance

name: Characterize the Land Degradation of Agricultural Land
description: Assess the state, extent, and severity of land degradation by identifying physical, chemical, and biological deterioration processes - such as soil erosion, salinization, and loss of biodiversity - to determine the reduction in the land's capacity to provide ecosystem services over time.
Related activities: Monitor LDN Achievement and Validate Progress Define Priority Areas of Intervention

name: Characterize Land and Soil Resources and Uses
description: Conduct a systematic inventory of land-based natural capital by analyzing soil properties, topography, and vegetative cover to establish a comprehensive spatial database for Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) planning. Classify land units and land types based on inherent land potential—determined by soil texture, depth, mineralogy, and thermal climates—to ensure a scientific basis for matching land-use requirements with biophysical limitations.

name: Characterize Water Resources
description: Establish a comprehensive inventory of blue and green water resources by analyzing precipitation, evapotranspiration, and hydrological regimes at the watershed or basin level. Implement water accounting and auditing to systematically document stocks, flows, and fluxes to underpin Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM). Characterize water stress, water scarcity, and historical drought frequency across different production systems.

name: Characterize the land and soil Management
description: Assess current land practices - including agronomic, vegetative, structural, and management measures - to determine their impact on resource sustainability and productivity. This involves documenting existing approaches, such as conservation agriculture, agroforestry, or grazing management, and evaluating their effectiveness in maintaining ecosystem functions, controlling degradation, and supporting livelihoods.
Related activities: Monitor Sustainable Land and Soil Management Performance

name: Characterize Land productivity, suitability and potential
description: Evaluate the capacity of land resources to support specific land utilization types by matching crop and livestock requirements with agro-climatic and edaphic conditions to determine attainable yields and production gaps. This process involves using land evaluation protocols to classify land suitability - from prime to unsuitable - under different management scenarios, thereby identifying opportunities to optimize resource use efficiency without compromising ecosystem functions. Crucially, integrate projected climate impacts and future land-use scenarios by utilizing advanced tools like GAEZ v5 and Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) to anticipate geographic shifts in land suitability

name: Analyze Socio-Economic Context, Gender, and Vulnerability of farmers and pastoralists
description: Conduct a comprehensive gender-sensitive analysis of the socioeconomic environment by examining livelihood strategies, access to productive resources, and tenure security to understand how structural inequalities shape the differential vulnerability of men, women, and youth to shocks and stresses. This entails examining power dynamics and resource control to ensure that interventions address the specific constraints faced by marginalized groups and strengthen their adaptive capacity against climate and economic instability.

name: Characterize Land Uses and Stakeholders
description: Map and describe current land use systems and the associated actors by integrating biophysical land cover data with socioeconomic attributes to understand human-environment interactions and conflicting interests regarding resource management. This involves identifying all direct and indirect stakeholders and analyzing their rights, responsibilities, and power relations through participatory methods to ensure that planning processes are inclusive and reflect the diverse needs and aspirations of those managing the land.

name: Conduct an integrated causal analysis by crossing biophysical, socio-economic, and management data to identify the direct and indirect drivers of land degradation
description: Utilize the Driver–Pressure–State–Impact–Response (DPSIR) framework to establish clear causal links between human activities (e.g., unsustainable management practices, population growth, land tenure insecurity) and the deteriorating state of land, soil, and water resources. Utilize Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to overlay spatial trends in global indicators—such as Soil Organic Carbon (SOC), Net Primary Productivity (NPP), and Land Cover Change (LCC)—with socio-economic variables like poverty levels, access rights, and market infrastructure. This 'convergence of evidence' approach allows to distinguish between natural environmental fluctuations and human-induced degradation, pinpointing degradation hotspots where urgent intervention is required.

name: Vulnerability and resilience Assessment
description: Conduct comprehensive vulnerability and resilience assessments to identify at-risk populations and ecosystems that are most susceptible to harm. This involves analyzing the unique combination of exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity within the specific socio-ecological system to determine where interventions will be most effective.

name: Setting Early Warning Systems
description: Establish and operationalize multi-hazard monitoring and early warning systems that integrate meteorological, agricultural, and livelihood data to detect emerging threats—such as drought, pests, and climate variability—before they escalate into crises

name: Define Vision & Objectives for the Landscape(s)
description: Develop a long-term, shared vision for the target landscape(s) based on validated information from the LDN targets assessment and aligned with (LDN) principles and national targets.
Related activities: Characterize the Land DegradationAssess and Ensure Cross-Sectoral Policy Coherence with competing land uses

name: Define Priority Areas of Intervention
description: Locate areas where land degradation is most urgent and where interventions will be most effective. It involves mapping current and potential degradation, validating existing hotspots through stakeholder workshops, and reviewing datasets, land-use contexts, drivers of degradation, while also taking into account areas affected by conflicts. Anticipate future degradation, identify priority areas for sustainable land management interventions, and ensure alignment with the shared LDN vision and validated assessment data.
Related activities: Characterize the Land DegradationCharacterize Land Uses and Stakeholders

name: Identification and Prioritisation of SLM practices
description: Compile a context-specific set of SLM practices that integrates scientific evidence with indigenous and traditional knowledge  systems with demonstrated potential to address identified degradation, causes and their  drivers. Assess their effects on key ecosystem services and their short- and long-term costs and benefits, while validating the effectiveness of local and customary approaches,,. Identify any additional suitable practices and prioritise all relevant options through a participatory process that fosters the co-creation of knowledge to address priority areas and underlying LD drivers.
Related activities: Characterize the land and soil ManagementAnalyze Socio-Economic Context, Gender, and Vulnerability of farmers and pastoralists

name: Design and Spatial Prioritisation of SLM Interventions
description: Link SLM practices to Priority Areas, evaluate their feasibility, and determine where and when they should be implemented. The activity includes preparing a matrix of suitable practices with priority areas, selecting and analysing top-prioritised options, assessing their costs for project-level implementation, and allocating them spatially using GIS. It also identifies lower-priority areas where practices can be phased in later or used as counterbalancing options.

name: Implementation roadmap
description: Develop a detailed implementation roadmap that specifies roles, responsibilities, locations, timelines, and modalities for carrying out the selected interventions. Validate this roadmap through a multi-stakeholder workshop to review and confirm roles, responsibilities, and timelines, and to identify potential barriers and corresponding solutions using the Landscape Matrix.

name: Monitor LDN Achievement
description: Establish and implement robust monitoring systems that track Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) status by measuring trends in land cover, land productivity, and carbon stocks against a fixed baseline to determine net gains and losses. To ensure accuracy, global datasets should be validated with national data, field assessments, and participatory inputs from local stakeholders to confirm that observed changes accurately reflect ground conditions.
Related activities: Characterize the Land DegradationDefine Vision & Objectives for the Landscape(s)e

name: Monitor Sustainable Land and Soil Management Performance
description: Assess and track the performance of sustainable land management practices by measuring soil organic carbon stocks, soil health, and land productivity dynamics to verify the effectiveness of interventions. This involves utilizing standardized protocols and integrating scientific data with local knowledge to evaluate improvements in biomass production, nutrient cycling, and water use efficiency, ensuring that agricultural intensification remains sustainable. “Agroecological transition evaluation,” emphasizing the need to track progress across the 10 Elements, combine biophysical and social indicators (such as tenure security, equity, and knowledge networks), and use monitoring as an adaptive, iterative redesign process.
Related activities: Characterize the Land ManagementPromote Sustainable Land Management and cropping diversity

name: Monitor Sustainable Productivity
description: Assess the long-term viability of agricultural systems by measuring Total Factor Productivity (TFP) and resource use efficiency - rather than solely relying on single-crop yields - to ensure that production gains do not compromise natural capital or ecosystem services.  This approach extends traditional accounting to explicitly include non-marketed environmental goods and services, such as soil health and water availability, while also accounting for negative externalities like pollution.
Related activities: Characterize Land productivity, suitability and potential

name: Monitor Social Impacts and Equity
description: Implement comprehensive assessment frameworks to monitor the socio-economic impacts of land use changes, focusing on food security,nutrition, gender equality, and the resilience of vulnerable communities to climate shocks. This involves using resilience diagnostic tools and disaggregated data to evaluate the capacity of households to absorb and recover from stresses, ensuring that land-based interventions support livelihoods and do not exacerbate existing inequalities.
Related activities: Analyze Socio-Economic Context, Gender, and Vulnerability of farmers and pastoralists

name: Monitor governance of tenure
description: Develop and apply participatory monitoring frameworks to assess the security of tenure and the recognition of legitimate rights, particularly for indigenous peoples and local communities. This involves using tools such as participatory mapping and community-led registries to document resource access, track the implementation of legal reforms, and identify emerging conflicts over natural resources to prevent dispossession and ensure equitable governance.
Related activities: Legally Recognize and Respect All Legitimate Tenure Rights

name: Monitor vulnerability and resilience
description: Establish a dynamic monitoring system to track the progress of resilience-building activities and assess the evolving capacity of your agrifood system to absorb, recover from, and transform in the face of shocks.

name: Monitor early warning
description: Establish a continuous monitoring framework that functions as a repository for climate data, drought indicators, and socio-economic variables to detect 'weak signals' of emerging threats before they escalate into crises
